earlier_scan.source_named: Glottolog Glottolog's most extensive descriptions are wordlists only (Loving & Bass 1964; Laycock 1973; Seiler 1985; Smits & Voorhoeve 1994); no grammar or phonology of Daonda located

sources.citation: Voorhoeve, C. L. 1971. Miscellaneous notes on languages in West Irian, New Guinea. In T. Dutton, C. L. Voorhoeve & S. A. Wurm, Papers in New Guinea Linguistics No. 14, 47-114. Pacific Linguistics A-28. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: Nothing about Daonda; classificatory mention only. (Sko is described as tonal with three tones -- unrelated language.)

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.3 languoid record and reference list for daon1243 (10 refs, none of doctype grammar/grammar sketch/phonology).
sources.note: Bibliographic only: Loving & Bass 1964 (8 pp.), Laycock 1973, Seiler 1985 app. A, Steer 2005, Smits & Voorhoeve 1994 (Anceaux wordlists), Laycock notebooks D1/D12, Ethnologue, WOLP, LL-MAP.

sources.citation: Klamer, Marian & Francesca R. Moro (eds.). 2023. Traces of Contact in the Lexicon: Austronesian and Papuan Studies. Leiden/Boston: Brill. DOI 10.1163/9789004529458. (incl. ch. 6: Schapper, Antoinette & Juliette Huber, 'Entwined Histories: The Lexicons of Kawaimina and Maka Languages', 180-209; ch. 8: Gerstner-Link, Claudia, 'Multilateral Lexical Transfer among Four Papuan Language Families: Border, Nimboran, Sentani, and Sko', 263-306; ch. 3 Klamer on Timor-Alor-Pantar/Austronesian contact, 57-100; ch. 5 Fricke on Lamaholot, 140-179; ch. 7 Moro, Sulistyono & Kaiping on Alorese, 213-262.)
sources.note: Named in the family table only; no phonology.

sources.citation: OLAC Nightly Data Dump 2021-07-18 (Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.5112131): all 5 records tagged olac:code="dnd" (Ethnologue page; Rosetta Project Swadesh list; PARADISEC DL2-023 Laycock Series D notebook pp.1592-1735 Waris/Simog/Daonda; Glottolog page; LINGUIST List page).
sources.note: Nothing; establishes that SIL Language & Culture Archives held zero items for dnd in 2021 (same dump has 74 SIL items for Amanab, 7 for Waris incl. their OPDs), i.e. no Daonda OPD/phonology exists in the SIL archive.

sources.citation: Ethnologue: Languages of the World, 17th edition (2013) and 19th edition (2016), entry 'Daonda [dnd]' (the Internet Archive captures of www.ethnologue.com/language/dnd, 2013-04-23, and /language/dnd/19, 2016-08-15).
sources.source_kind: database or survey citing another work
sources.note: Nothing: the entry has no Typology field. Content: Population 170 (2003 SIL); Location Sandaun Province, Amanab district near Imonda; Status 6b (Threatened); Classification Border, Waris; Language Use 'Adults understand Waris [wrs]' (19th: 'Also use Waris [wrs]'); 19th adds only OLAC/Language Cloud links. The '(2003 SIL)' population credit implies an SIL census/survey contact in 2003, but no SIL survey report for Daonda is indexed anywhere reachable (SIL-PNG code index has no dnd; OLAC 2021 dump 0 SIL items).

sources.citation: Steer, Martin. 2005. Languages of the Upper Sepik and Central New Guinea. Report prepared for the Upper Sepik-Central New Guinea Project (edits and Appendix 9.2 by B. Craig 2011). 60 pp.
sources.source_kind: database or survey citing another work
sources.note: nothing: classification, lexicostatistic percentages and four pronouns only

sources.citation: Carrington, Lois. 1996. A linguistic bibliography of the New Guinea area. Pacific Linguistics D-90. Canberra: Research School of Pacific and Asian Studies, ANU. (Daonda: Loving & Bass 1964 entry; Brown/Seiler entries for Waris/Imonda.)
sources.note: No phonology content (bibliography). Confirms that as of 1996 the only work covering Daonda directly was Loving & Bass 1964 (8 pp. survey); Waris-family phonology MSS listed are Brown 1974 'Tentative statement of Waris phonemes' and Brown n.d. 'Waris phonology' (Waris only).

sources.citation: Seiler, Walter. 1985. Imonda, a Papuan language. Pacific Linguistics B-93. Canberra: ANU. (sec. 1.1 pp.2-3; Appendix A 'Imonda and related languages' pp.210-218)
sources.note: Nothing about Daonda stress. Daonda appears only as a wordlist column (App. A.1) and in comparative example sentences (19)-(23); p.3 notes Daonda and Imonda may be more closely related to each other than either is to Waris. (The book's stress statement, p.10, is about Imonda only.)

sources.citation: Voorhoeve, C. L. 1975. Central and western Trans-New Guinea Phylum languages. In Wurm (ed.), New Guinea area languages and language study vol. 1, PL C-38; sec. 2.6.2.2.11.2.1.3 p.416.
sources.note: Nothing; one demographic sentence on Daonda (135 speakers, most similar to Imonda dialect of Waris). Phoneme lists given only for Waris and Manem, no stress statement for any Waris-family language.

sources.citation: Laycock, Donald C. 1973. Sepik languages: checklist and preliminary classification. Pacific Linguistics B-25. Entry 175 Daonda, pp.46-47.
sources.note: Nothing; village, population 135, data sources (test DCL70, SIL lists, Loving & Bass 1964); 'Many forms are close to the Imonda dialect of Waris.'
Stub: classification, villages, Ethnologue population; no phonology.

sources.note: 198-line IPA wordlist, no stress marks, no prose.
